title: Plurals: One Thing or Many
situation: Foundation: making Dutch nouns plural with -en, -s and -'s, the spelling shifts that come with -en, the units that stay singular after a number, and the short list of irregulars.
skills: choosing -en, -s or -'s by the final sound
the spelling shifts (doubling, dropping, f to v, s to z)
units that stay singular after a number

phrases.hindi: Ik heb twee broers en een zus.
phrases.english: I have two brothers and one sister.
phrases.context: `broer` ends in -r so the plural is -s. A very common way to open a conversation about family.
phrases.pronunciation: ik HEP TWAY BROORS en un ZUS

phrases.context: `kind` is irregular: `kinderen`. Note that the plural takes `de` even though `het kind` is a het-word.

phrases.english: How many languages do you speak?
phrases.context: `de taal` becomes `de talen`: the long vowel written twice drops one letter.

phrases.english: My grandmother has a lot of photos.
phrases.context: Both words end in a single vowel letter, so both take -'s.

phrases.hindi: Ik woon hier al drie jaar.
phrases.english: I have been living here for three years.
phrases.context: After a number, a unit of time stays singular. Never `drie jaren`.
phrases.pronunciation: ik WOHN heer al DREE YAAR

phrases.hindi: Er liggen twee brieven op tafel.
phrases.english: There are two letters on the table.
phrases.context: `brief` becomes `brieven`: the f turns into a v between vowels.
phrases.pronunciation: er LIG-gen TWAY BREE-ven op TAA-fel

phrases.hindi: De huizen in deze straat zijn oud.
phrases.english: The houses in this street are old.
phrases.context: `huis` becomes `huizen`: the s turns into a z. One of the most quoted examples in Dutch.
phrases.pronunciation: de HOW-zen in DAY-ze STRAAT zayn OWT

phrases.english: Could I have two cups of coffee?
phrases.context: Every small-and-cute `-je` form takes -s. You will order something this way most days.
Money after a number stays singular, so you hear `vijf euro`, never `vijf euros`.

grammar_notes: `-en` is the default plural ending. `-s` is used after an unstressed `-el`, `-em`, `-en`, `-er` or `-je`.
Nouns ending in a single vowel letter (a, i, o, u, y) take `-'s`: `oma's`, `foto's`, `menu's`. A final `-e` does not: `tante` becomes `tantes`.

Adding `-en` can change the spelling: double the consonant after a short vowel (`man` to `mannen`), drop one vowel when it was written twice (`boot` to `boten`), `f` becomes `v` (`brief` to `brieven`), `s` becomes `z` (`huis` to `huizen`).
Every plural noun takes `de`, whatever article the singular had. `het kind` but `de kinderen`.
After a number, units of measurement stay singular: `drie jaar`, `twee uur`, `vijf euro`, `vier kilo`.
culture_notes: Dutch uses the small-and-cute `-je` form far more than English uses any equivalent, so `-s` plurals turn up constantly in everyday speech: `kopjes`, `broodjes`, `kaartjes`.
Saying `drie jaren` instead of `drie jaar` is understood but marks you out immediately, because the singular form is so fixed in daily speech.
Because every plural is a de-word, going plural is a legitimate escape hatch when you genuinely cannot remember whether a noun is de or het.

skill_breakdown.skill: picking the ending from the final sound
skill_breakdown.explanation: Say the singular out loud. If it ends in an unstressed -el, -em, -en, -er or -je, add -s. If it ends in a single vowel letter, add -'s. Otherwise add -en, which is the default and covers most nouns.

skill_breakdown.skill: the spelling shifts that come with -en
skill_breakdown.explanation: Dutch spelling protects the vowel sound. A short vowel needs its consonant doubled, a long vowel written twice loses a letter, and f and s soften to v and z between vowels. These are the same habits that govern the present tense.

more_examples.breakdown: short vowel, so double the s
long vowel, so drop one a

skill_breakdown.explanation: After a number, measurements of time, money and weight stay singular. Separately, a short list of very common nouns is irregular and has to be learned whole, most of them in the -eren group.

more_examples.hindi: Ik heb tien euro bij me.
more_examples.english: I have ten euros on me.

practice_prompt:
You are a warm, patient Dutch tutor drilling plural formation with an A1 learner, one item at a time. Use `je` throughout, since this is a friendly tutoring session rather than an official one.

Open with exactly this line: "Hoi! Vandaag oefenen we het meervoud. Ik geef je een woord, jij maakt er het meervoud van. Klaar? Eerste woord: de stoel."

Work through roughly eight items, one per turn, and after each answer say whether it was right and why in one short sentence, then give the next word. Start easy and build: a plain -en word (de stoel, de trein), then an -s word (de tafel, de bakker), then a -je word (het kopje), then one that needs a spelling shift (de man, de boot, de brief, het huis), then an apostrophe word (de foto, de oma), then a unit after a number (ask: hoe zeg je 'three years'?), and finish with an irregular (het kind).

Keep your Dutch at A1: short sentences, everyday words, and always give the English in brackets for any instruction that is not obvious. Praise specifically rather than generically, for example "Goed, je hebt de f in een v veranderd."

When the learner makes a real mistake, tag it exactly like this so the app can log it:
[[CORRECTION: original="briefen" correct="brieven" reason="the f turns into a v between vowels"]]
Do not tag a typo or a missing capital. Only tag a genuine plural error.

After the last item give a one-line score, name the one pattern they should review, and end warmly.

theory.intro: You already know that Dutch nouns come with `de` or `het`. Now for the happier half of the story: what happens when there is more than one of something. Dutch has just two plural endings, the choice between them is decided by sound rather than by memory, and once a noun goes plural the de/het problem vanishes completely, because every plural takes `de`.

sections.heading: Two endings do almost all the work
sections.body:
Dutch has two plural endings, and between them they cover nearly every noun you will meet:
- **`-en`** is the default. Most nouns take it.
- **`-s`** is the alternative, used after a short list of endings.

So `de stoel` (the chair) becomes `de stoelen`, and `de tafel` (the table) becomes `de tafels`.

There is one piece of very good news here. **Every plural takes `de`**, with no exceptions. `het kind` is a het-word, but `de kinderen` is a de-word. So the moment a noun goes plural, the de/het problem disappears.

callout.body: If you are ever stuck, guess `-en`. It is the default and it is right far more often than `-s`.

sections.cutting_intro: Two endings, -en and -s, and one lovely rule: every plural is a de-word. Let me show you.

quick_check.question: Which article does a plural noun always take?
quick_check.explanation: Every Dutch plural takes de, even when the singular was a het-word.

sections.heading: Which ending? Listen to the last sound
sections.body:
You do not have to memorise lists. The ending is decided by **how the singular word finishes**.

Take **`-s`** when the word ends in an unstressed `-el`, `-em`, `-en`, `-er` or `-je`:
- `de tafel` becomes `de tafels`
- `de bezem` becomes `de bezems`
- `de jongen` becomes `de jongens`
- `de bakker` becomes `de bakkers`
- `het kopje` becomes `de kopjes`

That last one matters a lot, because **every small-and-cute `-je` form takes `-s`**, and Dutch makes those constantly.

Everything else takes **`-en`**: `de man` becomes `de mannen`, `het boek` becomes `de boeken`, `de vriend` becomes `de vrienden`.

examples.hindi: Ik heb twee broers en drie zussen.
examples.english: I have two brothers and three sisters.
examples.breakdown: `broer` ends in -r so it takes -s; `zus` is an ordinary word so it takes -en, with a doubled s.

examples.hindi: De kinderen spelen met de buren.
examples.english: The children are playing with the neighbours.

sections.cutting_intro: You never have to guess blindly. Say the word out loud and listen to how it ends. That is what picks the ending.

quick_check.question: What is the plural of het kopje (the little cup)?
quick_check.explanation: Words ending in -je always take -s, so het kopje becomes de kopjes.

sections.heading: The spelling shifts when you add -en
sections.body:
Adding `-en` can force a spelling change, because Dutch spelling protects the **sound** of the vowel. There are four patterns, and you already met three of them in the present tense.

- **Short vowel, so double the consonant.** `de man` becomes `de mannen`. Without the extra n, `manen` would be read with a long a.
- **Long vowel written twice, so drop one.** `de boot` becomes `de boten`. The vowel is already long in an open syllable, so the second o is not needed.
- **An f turns into a v.** `de brief` becomes `de brieven`.
- **An s turns into a z.** `het huis` becomes `de huizen`.

Those last two look odd at first, but they follow the ear: between two vowels Dutch prefers the softer sound.

callout.body: These are the same spelling habits that decide `ik werk` and `wij werken`. Learn them once and they pay off in the verbs too.

sections.cutting_intro: Adding -en sometimes changes the spelling. It is not random: Dutch is protecting the vowel sound.

quick_check.question: What is the plural of de brief (the letter)?
quick_check.explanation: The f turns into a v between vowels, giving brieven.

sections.heading: The apostrophe group, and numbers that stay singular
sections.body:
A small group of nouns ends in a **single vowel letter** `a`, `i`, `o`, `u` or `y`. Those take **`-'s`**, with an apostrophe, so the vowel does not get swallowed:
- `de oma` becomes `de oma's`
- `de foto` becomes `de foto's`
- `de baby` becomes `de baby's`
- `het menu` becomes `de menu's`

Words ending in an `-e` are not in this group: `de tante` simply becomes `de tantes`.

Then there is a habit that surprises English speakers. After a number, **units of measurement stay singular**:
- `drie jaar` (three years)
- `twee uur` (two hours)
- `vijf euro` (five euros)
- `een kilo` and `twee kilo`

You say `Ik woon hier drie jaar`, never `drie jaren`.

examples.hindi: Mijn oma heeft veel foto's van vroeger.
examples.english: My grandmother has a lot of photos from the past.
examples.breakdown: Both `oma` and `foto` end in a single vowel, so both take -'s.

examples.hindi: Ik werk hier al vier jaar.
examples.english: I have been working here for four years.
examples.breakdown: `jaar` is a unit after a number, so it stays singular.

sections.cutting_intro: Two small groups left. Words ending in a single vowel take an apostrophe, and measurements after a number do not change at all.

quick_check.question: How do you say five euros in Dutch?
quick_check.explanation: Units of measurement stay singular after a number, so it is vijf euro.

sections.heading: The irregulars worth learning
sections.body:
A handful of very common nouns do their own thing. There are not many, and you will use all of them, so learn them as whole words rather than trying to derive them.

The `-eren` group is the main one. These add a whole extra syllable:
- `het kind` becomes `de kinderen`
- `het ei` becomes `de eieren`

A second group changes its vowel:
- `de stad` becomes `de steden`
- `het schip` becomes `de schepen`

And `de koe` becomes `de koeien`, where a y-sound appears to keep the two vowels apart.

That really is the bulk of it. Everything else follows the rules above.

callout.body: Say `de kinderen` out loud a few times now. It is one of the most frequent nouns in the language and it is worth having automatic.

sections.cutting_intro: Last stop: the handful of irregulars. The good news is the list is short and you will use every word on it.

quick_check.question: What is the plural of het kind?
quick_check.explanation: Kind is in the -eren group, and like every plural it takes de.

theory.wrap_up: That is the whole system. Add `-en` by default, add `-s` after an unstressed `-el`, `-em`, `-en`, `-er` or `-je`, and add `-'s` after a single vowel letter. Watch for the four spelling shifts, leave measurements singular after a number, and learn the short irregular list as whole words. Best of all, every plural you make is a de-word, so half the article problem disappears the moment you pluralise.
